chunks.content: Introduction There is increasing trend of acute kidney injury (AKI) after myocardial infarction (MI), with incidence varying from 18.7% [ ] to 26% [ ]. AKI after MI has significant prognostic impact, being associated with prolonged hospital stay and increased short and long-term mortality [ – ]. AKI after MI also increases incidence of complications and is independently associated with higher risk of ESRD and death particularly in elderly population [ , ]. Multiple independent risk factors for AKI after MI have been identified, including age > 60 years, CHF, sepsis, undergoing coronary angiography (CAG) or Per-cutaneous intervention (PCI), low baseline eGFR, prolonged procedure time, time to coronary perfusion, high CK-MB at presentation, low systolic blood pressure, cardiogenic shock [ , , – ]. Other risk factors such as high total leukocyte count, low hematocrit have also been associated with higher AKI incidence after AMI [ , ]. However, findings from other settings may not fully apply to developing nations such as such as Nepal, Sub-Saharan and African, largely due to the limited and uneven distribution of PCI centers (currently only 11 nationwide in Nepal). This scarcity creates significant challenges for patient to seek medical attention at PCI centers within critical window period of the first few hours of symptom onset, resulting in delays in receiving reperfusion therapy [ – ]. Such delay likely increases the risk of MI related complications, including AKI [ ]. The timing of hospital presentation may influence AKI development and risk factors through mechanisms such as hemodynamic instability and inflammatory responses. Early presenters may experience acute hypoperfusion by myocardial necrosis, whereas delayed presenters may allow progression of myocardial injury, further worsens cardiac function, and may heighten the risk of AKI to nephrotoxic insults [ ]. We hypothesize that delayed presentation may modify the impact of other risk factors on AKI development. This study aims to investigate incidence and risk factors of Acute Kidney Injury (AKI) following MI in the western region of Nepal, with special consideration of impact of time of presentation after onset of symptoms on various risk factors. To our knowledge, the impact of timing of presentation on risk factors for AKI development after MI has not been previously investigated, representing a novel research gap in this field Methodology A hospital-based prospective cohort study was conducted among patients admitted to the Cardiology Department of Manipal Teaching Hospital, Pokhara Nepal with a confirmed diagnosis of myocardial infarction (MI) from 1 st December 2023 to 31 st October 2024. Ethical approval was obtained from the Institutional Review Committee of Manipal College of Medical Sciences, Pokhara (approval IRC/MCOMS/579) and written informed consent was obtained from all participants. Sample size The sample size was calculated using the formula for prospective cohort study, considering variables used in multivariate logistic regression, N = 10 ×K/P, where K is number of independent predictors and P is proportion of patients with the outcome (AKI). Considering the value of K as 6 [ ], and P as 0.48 [ ], the required sample size was 125. Sampling method The study employed non probability, consecutive sampling method, including all the eligible patients diagnosed with myocardial infarction admitted to cardiology department of Manipal Teaching hospital. Inclusion criteria Newly diagnosed case of Micas per American Heart Association Joint Committee (AHA/ACC) [ ] i.e. one of the five following predefined criteria should be satisfied before a diagnosis of MI is made: Symptoms of myocardial ischemia New/presumably new significant ST-segment/T-wave changes or left bundle branch block Development of new pathological Q waves on ECG New loss of viable myocardium or regional wall motion abnormality by imaging; Identification of intracoronary thrombus by angiography. Exclusion criteria Patient unwilling to give consent for participation in study. Patients who left the hospital against medical advice or were transferred to another healthcare facility. AKI definition, baseline serum creatinine and monitoring Patients were observed during hospitalization and categorized into two groups according to KDIGO criteria: Group 1: Patients who developed AKI after MI. Group 2: Patients who did not develop AKI after MI. For diagnosis of AKI after MI KDIGO criteria states: rise in serum creatinine > 0.3 mg/dl in window time of 48 hours or rise in serum creatinine more than 1.5 times over baseline serum creatinine or urine output < 0.5 ml/kg/hour over 6 hours [ ]. In this study, we applied serum creatinine criteria for development of AKI. Baseline serum creatinine was determined using recent documented pre-admission values whenever available. If no prior value was available, the initial serum creatinine at the time of admission was taken as baseline. Consistent with KDIGO guidance, when the admission serum creatinine appeared elevated, the lowest measured during hospitalization or post-treatment was used as baseline serum creatinine [ ]. Serial monitoring of creatinine was done every 24 hours during the inpatient stay until discharge

Baseline serum creatinine was determined using recent documented pre-admission values whenever available. If no prior value was available, the initial serum creatinine at the time of admission was taken as baseline. Consistent with KDIGO guidance, when the admission serum creatinine appeared elevated, the lowest measured during hospitalization or post-treatment was used as baseline serum creatinine [ ]. Serial monitoring of creatinine was done every 24 hours during the inpatient stay until discharge to evaluate change in renal function during the course of disease and treatment. The primary outcome of the study was development of AKI after MI and secondary outcomes included the hospital stay duration, complication rates and mortality. The main exposures examined were demographic characteristics, clinical presentation, laboratory values and procedural factor. Potential predictors included old age, delayed presentation, higher KILLIP class, reduced ejection fraction, elevated blood sugar levels and use of diuretics. Comorbidities such as hypertension, diabetes mellitus, history of previous myocardial infarction, alcohol consumption, and smoking status were considered as potential confounders. These were accounted for in multivariate logistic regression to isolate the independent effects of each predictor on the development of AKI. The timing of hospital presentation (≤12 hours vs. >12 hours after symptom onset) was identified as an effect modifier that influenced the relationship between certain predictors (e.g., male sex, diuretic use) and the risk of AKI. Bias reducing strategy Several measures were taken to minimize bias in the conduct of this study. To reduce selection bias, we applied clear and objective inclusion and exclusion criteria, enrolling consecutive eligible patients diagnosed with myocardial infarction during the study period. To avoid information bias, standardized protocols were used to collect clinical data, laboratory tests, and procedural details consistently across all participants regardless of their AKI status. Serum creatinine measurements for AKI diagnosis were performed using objective laboratory methods according to KDIGO guidelines. Confounding bias was addressed using multi-variate logistic regression and stratified analysis. Potential recall bias was minimized by relying on documented medical records for baseline characteristics and history instead of patient self-report alone. Loss to follow-up bias was limited by monitoring patients throughout hospitalization, and cases leaving against medical advice or transferred were excluded with clear documentation and reporting. Both significant as well as non-significant findings were adequately reported and thoroughly discussed to minimize reporting bias. Data collection and study variable Demographic information (age, sepsis, co-morbidities, smoking) and clinical data such as MI type and location, killip class, time from symptoms onset to presentation, vital signs i.e. heart rate, mean arterial pressure (MAP) were evaluated at the time of presentation. Laboratory evaluations such as hemoglobin, platelets, total leukocyte counts (TLC), serum albumin, CK-MB and troponin I were evaluated using venous blood at the time of presentation. Procedural and therapeutics data such as medications (beta blocker, diuretics, ACEI, IV fluids), use of contrast, contrast volume and angiography findings were subsequently recorded during the time of their hospitalization and management. The primary outcome was occurrence of AKI after MI (Yes/NO) as per KDIGO criteria. All the relevant risk factors from the collected data were evaluated for the development of AKI. Statistical analysis and pre-defined analysis plan A pre-defined statistical analysis plan (SAP) was developed prior to data analysis to ensure methodological transparency and minimize analytical bias. It outlined the study objectives, primary and secondary outcomes, and statistical methods to be used. The primary outcome was the development of AKI following myocardial infarction, defined by KDIGO criteria. Data were analyzed using SPSS version 25. Continuous variables are presented as mean with standard deviation and categorical variables as counts and percentage. Association between categorical variables and development of AKI were tested using Chi-Square and Fischer exact test with a p value < 0.05 considered statistically significant. Relative risks with 95% confidence intervals were calculated to evaluate the risk factors. Stratified analysis was done to evaluate impact of time of presentation after symptoms onset (<12 hrs. vs. >12 hrs.) on various risk factors by symptom duration assessed effect modification. Variables like Age, pack years of smoking (number of cigarettes per day * year of smoking/20), Time of presentation after symptoms onset, mean arterial pressure (MAP), heart rate (HR), total leukocyte count (TLC), hemoglobin (Hb), platelets, random blood sugar at the time of presentation (RBS), serum albumin, CK-MB, ejection fraction (EF) were analyzed using univariate logistic regression and all the variables which had p-value < 0.1 were considered for multivariate logistic regression model. Results A total of 131 patients were included, with a mean age of 60.92 ± 15.05 years, of whom 66.4% were male. Most of the cases were between age group 51–60 years (23.7%). The median time from symptom onset to hospital presentation was 12 hours (mean 35.14 ± 8.32 hours). Once at our center, mean door to needle time for PCI was 4.5 ± 2.2 hours as shown in Table and Fig. . Among 131 cases of MI, Anterior wall MI (56.48%) followed by inferior wall MI (28.24%) and STEMI (67.93%) were most common sub-type of MI. Majority of the cases presented with clinical mild symptoms and fall within Killip class I (41.98%). The relative risk analysis demonstrated that patient with reduced EF ( < 40%) had 2.19-fold and 3.03-fold higher risk of AKI development than that with mildly reduced EF (40%-50%) and preserved EF (>50%) respectively. Similarly, clinically severe MI (Killip class III and IV) had 2.95-fold higher risk of AKI development than that of milder form i.e. Killip class I as shown in Table . Among 131 cases analyzed, procedure requiring contrast such as coronary angiography (CAG) with or without PCI was only done 86 (65.64%) of cases, which reveals the most common coronary artery involved was RCA (62.59%), followed by LADA (35.87%) and Single vessel disease (SVD) was commonest form of coronary artery disease i.e. 54 (62.79% of cases undergoing CAG). The RR and p value indicated use of contrast > 100 ml was significantly associated with AKI development, it increases the risk of AKI development by 2.01-fold and 2.9-fold in comparison to < 100 ml and no use of contrast respectively as shown in Table . Ejection fraction, Killip class at the time of presentation, and contrast volume were found to be independent risk factor for AKI irrespective of the time of presentation i.e. p value < 0.05 was found in both of the sub groups divided in Table . However, the effect of gender and diuretics use as a risk factor to produce AKI post MI was dependent on time of presentation. Male sex was significantly associated with AKI only amongst patient presented within 12 hours of symptoms onset ( p value < 0.05), whereas diuretics use was only associated with AKI amongst patients presented after 12 hours. Thus, there was effect modification of time of presentation on gender and diuretics use as a risk factor for AKI shown by stratified analysis in Table . 12 variables i.e. age, pack years, duration of symptoms at the time of presentation, heart rate, mean arterial pressure (MAP),hemoglobin, platelets, total leukocyte count, serum albumin, RBS, CK-MB and EF were first analyzed using univariate logistic regression. Out of which 6 variables i.e. age, duration of symptoms at the time of presentation, heart rate, serum albumin, RBS and EF had p value < 0.1 which were selected for multivariate logistic regression as shown in Table . Multivariate analysis identified age > 60 years ( n = 68; 51.9%), symptom duration > 12 hours ( n = 66; 50.4%), random blood sugar > 200 mg/dL ( n = 49; 37.4%), ejection fraction < 40% ( n = 37; 28.2%), contrast volume > 100 ml ( n = 29; 22.1%), and diuretic use ( n = 38; 29.0%) as significant risk factors for acute kidney injury ( p < 0.05 for all), as shown in Table . This multivariate logistic regression had Hosmer and lameshow test ( p = 0.690) which indicates good model fit and Negelkerke R 2 = 0.552 which indicates moderate to strong model fit. These findings align with Zhou et al., Kalum et al., and James et al., who observed increased AKI risk among older individuals attributed to reduced renal adaptability linked to age related hemodynamic alterations and co-morbidities [ – ]. This robust association highlights the need for future research focused on age-specific preventive strategies, with the goal of identifying novel reno-protective interventions. Our study found that males exhibited significantly higher AKI incidence following MI compared to females (48.3% vs. 27.3%, χ 2 = 5.320, p = 0.02), further confirmed by continuity correction (χ 2 = 4.489, p = 0.034), likelihood ratio test (χ 2 = 5.477, p = 0.001), 95% CI relative Risk (RR) 1.12–2.44.These findings are consistent with other studies, who reported increased AKI risk in males attributed to sex-based renal physiology differences, higher burden of cardiovascular risk factors, increased hemodynamic instability, while estrogen is postulated to exert reno-protective effect in women [ , ]. Gender’s association with AKI depends on time of presentation. It was significant risk factor for AKI among patients presenting within 12 hours of symptoms onset ( p < 0.05), but not in those presenting beyond 12 hours ( p > 0.05). This indicates effect modification of gender’s impact on AKI by the timing of presentation. There was significant decrease incidence of AKI among female in comparison to male who were early presenters, where as this difference was not seen among late presenters as shown in Table . This novel effect modification may be explained by an experimental evidence demonstrating that female sex hormones blunt post-ischemic renal injury, whereas removal of estrogen (e.g. ovariectomy) worsens AKI markers after MI [ ]. Estrogen is known to enhance endothelial nitric oxide signaling, reduce inflammation and oxidative stress [ , ]. Thus, when patients present early, women’s hormonal advantage may afford protection and men’s relative risk becomes apparent. In contrast, delayed presentation with prolonged ischemia may overwhelm these sex-specific protective mechanisms, diminishing observable differences. This finding further hypothesize that early intervention and PCI in female may leads to more favorable renal outcome and fewer AKI-related complications compared with male. Although this proposed mechanism remains speculative and has not been previously reported, it highlights the need for future studies to investigate the interplay between sex hormones, hemodynamic factors and treatment timing jointly influence AKI risk after MI. Our study identified a significant association between delayed hospital presentation (≥12 hours after symptom onset) and increased incidence of AKI post MI (χ 2 = 35.545, p < 0.001), further supported by the continuity correction (χ 2 = 33.460, p < 0.001), likelihood ratio test (χ 2 = 37.714, p < 0.001), with strong correlation measures (Phi = 0.521, Cramer’s V = 0.521, p < 0.001) and logistic regression analysis (B = 0.029, p < 0.001, Odds Ratio = 1.030, 95% CI: 1.014–1.045) and (95% CI of RR 2.68–4.65). These findings confirmed, every hour of delays heightens AKI risk. These findings align with previous studies that have reported a significant rise in AKI risk with delayed treatment of acute MI [ , ]. Limited and uneven distribution of PCI facilities in Nepal (total 11), Sub-Saharan Africa, and other developing countries leads to delays in presentation for MI treatment ranging from hours to days [ – ]. These delays driven by limited PCI centers, geographic barriers are not uncommon. Thus, managing MI within the window period poses significant challenges in developing nation. This delay in presentations can leads to complications like arrhythmias, LV dysfunction and AKI. Yet, risk of AKI remains a neglected but critical concern in this scenarios [ ]. Addressing these challenges requires urgent focus on tailored strategies: expanding PCI access, enhancing risk assessment and innovating therapies suitable for low resource environments. Future researches that aim to find and implement such interventions may reduce AKI and improve overall outcome among MI cases in developing nations like Nepal. These findings are consistent with Goldberg et al. and Tziakas et al. who reported that higher Killip class increases AKI risk post-AMI. Their findings emphasize early recognition and management of cardiac dysfunction to prevent renal complications [ , ]. Future researches should explore targeted strategies to reduce AKI risk in patients with higher Killip classes, including aggressive hemodynamic stabilization and timely therapeutic interventions to improve clinical outcomes. Our study demonstrated a strong and significant association between EF category and AKI incidence (χ 2 = 25.981, df = 2, p < 0.001), confirmed by likelihood ratio test (χ 2 = 26.472, p < 0.001) and Linear-by-Linear association (13.806, p < 0.001) suggesting lower EF correlated with higher AKI risk, with moderate-to-strong correlation (ϕ = 0.445, p < 0.001; Cramer’s V = 0.445, p < 0.001). Further logistic regression analysis demonstrated an inverse relation between EF and AKI risk (B = −0.084, p = 0.002, OR = 0.919, 95% CI: 0.871–0.970) and (95% CI of RR 1.75 -3.71). These findings align with Hertzberg et al., who reported higher AKI incidence with reduced EF [ ]. However, Margolis et al. suggested that mid-range EF was not an independent predictor of AKI, contrasting with our results [ ]. This highlights the need for further research to determine whether EF alone or in conjunction with other cardiac parameters better predicts AKI risk. Our study found that contrast use alone was not significant predictor of AKI ( p > 0.05), but higher contrast volumes showed significant association with increased AKI risk (χ2 = 19.248, df = 1, p < 0.001), confirmed by linear-by-linear association ( p < 0.001) with moderate-to-strong association (ϕ = 0.473, p < 0.001, Cramer’s V = 0.473, p < 0.001). These results align with Amin et al. and Yuan et al., which emphasize that contrast volume plays a pivotal role in the development of contrast-induced nephropathy (CIN) or contrast-induced AKI (CI-AKI). Their findings highlight the need for patient-specific contrast volume thresholds and implementing nephron-protective strategies to reduce AKI risk particularly in high-risk patients undergoing contrast-based procedures [ , ]. Our study revealed a significant association between diuretic use and AKI (χ2 = 13.334, df = 1, p < 0.001) as shown in Table , effect size measures (ϕ = 0.319, p < 0.001 Cramer’s V = 0.319, p < 0.001) and 95% CI of RR 1.31–2.91, suggest a moderate effect, highlighting the clinical relevance of this finding. These results align with other studies, which reported that perioperative diuretic increases AKI risk in MI patients undergoing PCI [ ]. Importantly, diuretics use association with AKI is largely driven by time of presentation after onset of symptoms. Diuretics use was significant AKI risk factor only in patients presenting after 12 hours of symptoms onset ( p < 0.05), not in those presenting within 12 hours of symptoms onset ( p > 0.05) as shown in Table . This indicates effect modification by timing of presentation for diuretics use impact. This finding of use of diuretics among cases of MI based on duration of symptoms present is novel finding and no other study was found for comparing and correlating this effect modification. This increased risk observed in late presenters may be explained by ongoing myocardial injury and worsening congestion, which worsens cardiac output and renal perfusion over time. Diuretics use in these cases can precipitate prerenal AKI by further reducing circulatory volume. This is consistent with known pharmacology: diuretic induced hypovolemia and electrolyte shifts can precipitate or worsen AKI, especially in hemodynamically unstable patients [ ]. Clinically, these findings suggest that standard heart failure management with diuretics may carry extra renal risk if instituted after prolonged MI ischemia. It underscores the importance of cautious volume management and risk stratification in delayed presenters, and it generates new hypotheses about diuretic stewardship in this vulnerable subset. Although AKI incidence was slightly higher in diabetic patients (46.2%) compared to non-diabetics (40.0%), this difference was not significant (χ 2 = 0.326, p = 0.568). Measures of association, including Phi = 0.050, p = 0.568 and Cramer’s V = 0.050, p = 0.568, indicated a weak correlation. These findings align with Marenzi et al., who observed that despite poor cardiac and renal function in DM, it was not an independent AKI predictor [ ]. Li et al. reported that acute hyperglycemia, rather than DM alone, increased AKI risk in MI patients, consistent with our finding that poor glycemic control during hospitalization was associated with higher AKI incidence (χ 2 = 8.34, p < 0.05) irrespective of their history of DM [ ]. This suggests that stress-induced hyperglycemia plays crucial role in AKI development, highlighting importance of glycemic control as a potential intervention for AKI prevention irrespective of DM status. Similarly, AKI incidence was slightly higher in patients with prior history of MI (45.5% vs. 40.8%), regular alcohol consumers (45.9% vs. 39.4%) and smokers (43.4% vs. 39.7%) this difference was not statistically significant ( p value > 0.05), and suggesting prior MI, regular alcohol consumption and smokers may not be an independent predictor of AKI. These findings align with prior studies, which reported no significant association between prior MI, alcohol consumption and smoking with development of AKI, emphasizing the role of baseline renal function and hemodynamic stability as more critical determinants [ – ]. Conversely, few studies reported increased AKI risk with prior MI [ , ], and increased risk of post MI renal damage in experimental mouse model [ ]. Similarly, AKI was more common in STEMI (46.1%) than NSTEMI (31.0%) and in hypertensive patient (46.2%) than non-hypertensive (39.1%), it was not statistically significant ( p > 0.05). These findings align with other studies, which reported that AKI in MI patients, particularly those undergoing PCI, is influenced by factors such as hemodynamic instability and microvascular myocardial damage rather than solely by ECG classification and hypertension [ , ]. Conversely, other studies identified hypertension as an independent risk factor for AKI development, particularly in patients undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) [ , ]. Future research should investigate combined influence of alcohol consumption, smoking, ECG findings, hypertension on large sample study for AKI development post MI to determine whether the observed, though statistically insignificant increased risk of AKI meaningfully contributes to AKI prediction. Our study found no association between elevated WBC count (χ 2 = 0.762, p = 0.383, Troponin I levels (χ 2 = 0.128, df = 1, p = 0.721), anatomical MI type (χ2 = 1.395, df = 3, p = 0.707), involved coronary artery (χ 2 = 3.464, df = 3, p = 0.325) and number of coronary artery involved ( p value = 0.231) with development of AKI. This align with previous studies which attribute AKI development post-MI more to patient factors, hemodynamic instability and contrast exposure rather than WBC count, anatomical MI location or coronary artery involved [ , – ], where as in contrast to study done by Krzesi et al., who linked multi-vessel CAD may elevate AKI risk in MI patients [ ]. Although the use of ACE inhibitors (ACEI) demonstrated a lower incidence of AKI (20% vs. 43%) compared to non-use, and the administration of IV fluids also showed a modest reduction in AKI (30.8% v/s 42.4%), these Reno-protective effect of ACEI and IV fluids were statistically insignificant ( p value > 0.05). These findings align with other studies which suggest that while ACEIs have Reno-protective effects in chronic settings, their role in acute settings, particularly in AKI after MI, remains complex and inconclusive [ ]. Limitations of the study This is a single centric study and have smaller sample size ( n = 131). Thus, multi-centric study with larger sample size is required to validate this novel finding. Memory bias may lead to incorrect or incomplete history regarding the risk factors. This study specifically addresses the risk of AKI during hospitalization after MI and does not evaluate the long-term impact of MI on renal function. The objective of this study was to evaluate risk factor of AKI after MI and how timing of presentation affected those risk factors. Thus, the long term outcome and effect of AKI after MI was not evaluated. Although major co-morbidities are analyzed in this study, the complex interplay between these may alters patients’ outcome and development of AKI. Conclusion The incidence of AKI after MI in our study was 41.2%, which was relatively high and may be attributed to delayed hospital presentation. Risk factors significantly associated with increased AKI risk include age over 60 years, male sex, presentation beyond 12 hours after symptoms onset, higher Killip class (III and IV), reduced ejection fraction ( < 40%) and use of diuretics. Stratified analysis revealed that male sex was significant risk factor for AKI only among patients presenting within 12 hours, whereas diuretics use increased AKI risk only in those presenting after 12 hrs. This effect modification by time of presentation on sex and diuretics use is a novel finding and requires multicenter study for further confirmation. Elevated blood sugar during hospitalization was also associated with increased AKI risk regardless of diabetes status, while diabetes itself was not a significant risk factor. Although use of contrast was not associated with increased risk of AKI, higher contrast volume significantly increased AKI risk. The median time of hospital presentation was 12 hours, a pattern common in resource limited settings due to limited PCI availability. These measures, combined with optimized procedural and medical management, may reduce AKI incidence and improve outcomes in patients with MI.

chunks.content: 1 Introduction Heart failure (HF) represents a clinical syndrome defined by signs and symptoms arising from structural or functional cardiac abnormalities. Diagnosis is typically confirmed through elevated natriuretic peptide levels and/or objective signs of pulmonary or systemic congestion ( – ). HF represents a substantial threat to patients’ health and quality of life ( ). The likelihood of developing HF is considerably higher in those with coronary artery disease (CAD). When CAD and HF co-exist, they act together to drive up the rates of disability and mortality. Therefore, a concerted effort to manage CAD patients, specifically to prevent the onset of HF, is particularly crucial ( , ). Traditionally, the elevated risk of HF in patients with CAD has often been attributed to factors such as hypertension, poor blood pressure (BP) control, and suboptimal management of blood glucose and lipids ( – ). However, the role of obesity−driven insulin resistance (IR) in this process has not received sufficient attention ( ). CAD itself, characterized by atherosclerosis and luminal stenosis, is frequently accompanied by IR and various metabolic disorders, which may collectively exacerbate adverse clinical outcomes including HF ( , ). In recent years, the critical role of obesity and IR in the pathogenesis of multiple diseases—such as cardiovascular diseases, sepsis, and cancer—has garnered increasing attention ( – ). Against this backdrop, a series of novel indices reflecting metabolic status have emerged, among which the triglyceride−glucose (TyG) index and its derivatives [TyG-body mass index (TyG-BMI), TyG-waist circumference (TyG-WC)], as well as the metabolic score for IR (METS−IR), are the most commonly cited ( – ). These indices comprehensively reflect the degree of obesity, the state of IR, and the overall metabolic dysregulation, and have demonstrated considerable utility across various diseases ( , , ). For instance, studies have shown that TyG and its derived indices exhibit excellent predictive performance for stroke and cardiovascular mortality ( , ); in metabolic−associated fatty liver disease, these indices also perform well, suggesting their potential as early screening tools ( ). Notably, patients with CAD often present with multiple metabolic abnormalities. These interrelated metabolic disturbances significantly increase the risk of adverse outcomes, among which HF represents one of the most critical complications ( , ). Therefore, investigating the association between these obesity−metabolic indices and HF in patients with CAD holds important clinical relevance. This multicenter study was designed to systematically examine the associations between four obesity-metabolic indices—TyG, TyG-BMI, TyG-WC, and METS-IR—and the occurrence of HF in patients with CAD, as well as to explore their potential mediating mechanisms. The findings may provide a reference for weight management, assessment of IR-related metabolic disorders, and early identification of HF risk in this population. 2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study population This was a multicenter retrospective study. Initially, 4685 patients with confirmed CAD were enrolled from three hospitals: Changzhi People’s Hospital in Shanxi Province, Yunyang County People’s Hospital, and Xinxiang Central Hospital. After excluding 166 patients with incomplete baseline information, we further applied the following exclusion criteria: 1) severe hepatic or renal dysfunction; 2) active malignancy; 3) admission due to acute coronary syndrome; 4) recent coronary revascularization; and 5) admission for hypertensive crisis. Following this rigorous screening process, a total of 3872 patients were eligible and included in the final analysis. The detailed patient selection flow is presented in . This clinical observational study was conducted in strict accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. The study protocol was reviewed and approved by the Ethics Committees of Changzhi People’s Hospital (CZX20180213), Yunyang County People’s Hospital (Yy20200419), and Xinxiang Central Hospital (NXCH20230911). Continuous variables are presented as mean±standard deviation (SD) or median (interquartile range) depending on their distribution, while categorical variables are expressed as frequency and percentage. Multivariable-adjusted logistic regression was used to examine the associations between the four obesity-metabolic indices and HF. To assess the diagnostic utility of each obesity-metabolic index for HF, we utilized receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves, decision curve analysis (DCA), and variable importance ranking. Subgroup and sensitivity analyses were further performed to test the robustness of the primary outcomes. Mediation analysis was also conducted to examine whether the obesity-metabolic index influences HF onset through specific intermediary pathways. Detailed statistical procedures are described in the . All analyses were carried out with R software (version 4.4.3), adopting a two-sided P < 0.05 as the threshold for statistical significance. 3 Results 3.1 Comparison of baseline characteristics between HF and Non-HF groups Among the 3872 patients with CAD enrolled in this study, 806 were identified as having HF. Based on HF diagnosis, participants were categorized into two groups, with their baseline demographic and clinical features summarized in . In terms of general characteristics, the heart failure group had significantly higher BMI and DBP compared to the non-HF group. Laboratory test results showed that TG, LDL-C, eGFR, and BNP levels were also significantly higher in the HF group. Moreover, all four obesity-metabolic indexes were noticeably higher in the HF group. Regarding comorbidities and medication usage, the HF group had a higher prevalence of hypertension and hyperlipidemia. They were also more likely to be taking diuretics, beta-blockers, and ACEIs/ARBs ( ). No significant differences were observed between the two groups in other aspects. 3.2 Relationship between four obesity-metabolic indices and HF in patients with CAD To investigate the relationship between different obesity-metabolic indices and HF, we first divided the participants into four groups based on the quartiles of the four obesity-metabolic indices and compared the HF prevalence across these groups. The results were clear: for all four indices, the prevalence of HF gradually increased from the Q1 group to the Q4 group ( ). Next, we used logistic regression and established four models to adjust for covariates and assess the relationship between these indices and HF. The results indicated that in the unadjusted Model 1, for each 1 SD increase in the four obesity-metabolic indices—TyG, TyG-BMI, TyG-WC, and METS-IR—the odds of HF increased by 75.6% [odds ratio (OR):1.756, 95% confidence interval (CI):1.620-1.906], 104.8% (OR:2.048, 95%CI: 1.884-2.230), 154.3% (OR:2.543, 95%CI: 2.330-2.782), and 157.7% (OR:2.577, 95%CI: 2.355-2.826), respectively ( ). The results showed that compared to patients with values below or equal to the threshold, patients with TyG, TyG-BMI, TyG-WC, and METS-IR exceeding the identified thresholds of 8.27, 240, 520, and 38.5 had risks 2.444 (95%CI: 2.076-2.884), 2.759 (95%CI: 2.334-3.269), 4.027 (95%CI: 3.378-4.817), and 4.028 (95%CI: 3.379-4.819) times higher, respectively ( , ). This further underscores the strong association between elevated obesity-metabolic indices and the increased risk of HF in patients with CAD. Moreover, exceeding these thresholds significantly amplifies the risk. These findings highlight that controlling weight and reducing insulin resistance-related metabolic disturbances may help decrease the incidence of HF events. 3.4 Subgroup analysis and sensitivity analysis Considering that factors such as patients’ baseline characteristics, lifestyle habits, and disease status might influence the study results, we conducted subgroup analyses based on gender, age, BMI, smoking status, alcohol consumption, hypertension, diabetes, and hyperlipidemia. As shown in , all four obesity-metabolic indices remained significantly associated with HF risk across all subgroups, indicating that these relationships are independent of the stratification variables. To further evaluate the robustness of the main results, we performed multiple sensitivity analyses. Initially, we performed a subgroup analysis excluding patients with acute HF, as this population typically presents with more severe complications and complex metabolic disturbances that could confound the association between obesity-related metabolic indices and HF. After exclusion, the results remained materially consistent with those from the overall study population, indicating that the inclusion of acute HF patients did not significantly influence our primary findings ( ). Subsequently, to reduce potential confounding from advanced age, we excluded participants older than 75 years. The associations did not change materially ( ). Furthermore, given the pathophysiological differences between HF subtypes, we further examined the relationship between obesity-related metabolic indices and specific HF subtypes. The results demonstrated that elevated levels of these indices were significantly associated with both HF subtypes ( ). Finally, to account for potential residual confounding factors, we conducted an E-value analysis for unmeasured confounders. The results indicated that unmeasured confounding factors would need to be exceptionally large to overturn our findings ( ). 3.5 Comparison of the diagnostic performance of different obesity-metabolic indices for HF Considering that all four obesity-metabolic indices were closely associated with the occurrence of HF, we performed a series of comparative analyses to identify the best diagnostic indicator. First, we compared the indices using ROC curves. The results showed that all four indices demonstrated good diagnostic performance, with the area under the curve (AUC) for TyG, TyG-BMI, TyG-WC, and METS-IR all exceeding 0.65. Specifically, the AUCs were 0.656, 0.684, 0.731, and 0.751, respectively ( , ). Among them, METS-IR showed the best diagnostic ability, with both sensitivity and specificity being relatively good ( , ). To further assess the clinical utility of these indices, we performed DCA to evaluate their net benefit. The results consistently indicated that METS-IR provided the highest net benefit compared to the other three obesity-metabolic indices ( ). Additionally, we employed the Boruta algorithm to determine the variable importance of different indices in machine learning models. The findings were consistent with our previous analyses, demonstrating that METS-IR had the highest variable importance among all variables ( ). Finally, we compared the diagnostic capability of the obesity-metabolic indices with that of the traditional HF scoring system. The results revealed that METS-IR continued to outperform the traditional HF scoring system in diagnosing HF ( ). 3.6 Role of renal function in mediation To further explore the potential pathways through which obesity-metabolic indices may influence the occurrence of HF, we screened relevant variables and identified that eGFR likely plays a key mediating role ( ). Mediation analysis revealed that the four obesity-metabolic indices—particularly TyG-WC and METS-IR—partially mediated the development of HF by affecting eGFR, which reflects renal function, with mediation proportions of 7.27% and 7.74%, respectively ( ). This finding underscores the potential importance of anti-inflammatory strategies in mitigating obesity-related HF risk. Collectively, these mediation analyses suggest that both renal function impairment and systemic inflammation may serve as important intermediary mechanisms linking obesity-metabolic indices to the development of HF. 4 Discussion Current evidence has established that obesity-metabolic indices such as TyG, TyG-BMI, TyG-WC, and METS-IR are associated with various adverse outcomes including cardiovascular mortality, autoimmune diseases, sepsis, and cancer ( , – ). However, their relationship with HF in patients with CAD has not been sufficiently studied. Our multicenter study systematically demonstrates a significant association between these four indices and HF in patients with CAD, with a clear threshold effect observed. In particular, when TyG, TyG-BMI, TyG-WC, and METS-IR exceed 8.27, 240, 520, and 38.5 respectively, their association with HF becomes significantly stronger. Further analysis indicated that all four obesity-metabolic indices possess diagnostic value for HF, with METS-IR demonstrating the most outstanding overall performance. Mediation analysis further suggested that these indices, particularly METS-IR, may contribute to HF occurrence partly through impairing renal function. In conclusion, our findings highlight METS-IR as a superior obesity-metabolic indicator that not only assists in weight management and metabolic assessment in high-risk CAD populations but may also offer important clinical insights for early HF prevention through improving IR and preserving renal function. Patients with CAD represent a large, high-risk population, with a global prevalence exceeding 200 million. CAD remains a leading cause of mortality worldwide ( ). These individuals endure a multifaceted burden, including persistent symptoms such as angina and dyspnea, reduced quality of life, and a significantly elevated risk for major adverse cardiovascular events, such as myocardial infarction and stroke ( – ). A critical long-term complication of CAD is its progression to HF, with studies showing that nearly two-thirds of HF cases have underlying CAD ( , ). Key modifiable risk factors, including hypertension, dyslipidemia, diabetes, and smoking, contribute to both the progression of CAD and the onset of HF ( , ). Consequently, comprehensive management is crucial. This includes aggressive risk factor control, guideline-directed medical therapy such as SGLT2 inhibitors and ARNIs, and vigilant monitoring for early signs of HF decompensation, all of which are vital for improving survival and reducing the significant associated mortality ( , – ). Obesity-metabolic indices are increasingly being applied in the diagnosis and prediction of a growing number of diseases ( – ). A recent meta-analysis on the TyG index and CAD found that patients with a high TyG index have a 7.95 times higher risk of developing CAD compared to those with a low TyG index. This suggests that individuals with elevated TyG levels face significantly increased risks of developing CAD and stroke ( ). In a Japanese cross−sectional study, each 10−unit rise in TyG−BMI was associated with a 31% increase in hypertension prevalence, confirming a significant relationship between TyG−BMI and hypertension ( ). Analyses based on the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) database further demonstrated that a 1−unit increment in TyG−WC elevated the risk of cardiac death by 1.45−fold and diabetes−related mortality by 2.545−fold among individuals with metabolic syndrome ( ). Another NHANES−derived study reported that METS−IR was correlated with both all−cause and cardiovascular mortality, with a notably higher risk of all−cause mortality observed when METS−IR exceeded 41.33 ( ). Furthermore, a growing body of recent evidence underscores that the type of obesity, rather than just its presence, may exert differential effects on cardiovascular disease risk ( , ). It has been consistently demonstrated that central fat distribution, as opposed to peripheral adiposity, serves as a stronger predictor of cardiometabolic complications ( ). This suggests that the adverse metabolic and clinical impact is more closely linked to visceral fat accumulation than to overall or peripheral adiposity. These collective findings imply that IR and metabolic disturbances reflected by obesity−related indices may contribute to the pathogenesis of multiple conditions, including HF. This highlights the clinical relevance of weight control, obesity mitigation, and the management of IR−related metabolic dysregulation. METS-IR integrates multiple indicators reflecting obesity and metabolism, including FPG, triglycerides, BMI, and HDL-C. These metabolic parameters are closely associated with various diseases, including HF. Compared to single indicators, METS-IR, by combining these parameters, may more accurately reflect the overall metabolic status and IR level in the body. Therefore, its comprehensive nature likely contributes to its superior diagnostic capability in identifying HF. In the future, this simple and easily accessible tool may potentially be used for HF risk assessment and high-risk population screening among patients with CAD. The progression from CAD to HF is critically accelerated by underlying metabolic disturbances, primarily obesity and IR ( – ). These conditions create a synergistic pathological environment through several interconnected mechanisms. First, IR disrupts myocardial substrate metabolism, shifting energy production toward less efficient fatty acid oxidation and promoting the intracellular accumulation of toxic lipid intermediates. This accumulation induces cardiomyocyte apoptosis and mitochondrial dysfunction ( , , ). Second, dysfunctional visceral adipose tissue acts as an endocrine organ, secreting pro-inflammatory adipokines such as TNF-α and IL-6, which foster a state of chronic low-grade systemic inflammation ( – ). This inflammation contributes to coronary microvascular endothelial dysfunction and promotes direct myocardial fibrosis ( , ). Third, hyperinsulinemia and activation of the sympathetic nervous system lead to sodium retention, increased plasma volume, and hypertension, creating a chronic pressure overload that results in left ventricular hypertrophy and diastolic dysfunction ( – ). Collectively, these processes—metabolic derangement, inflammation, and neurohormonal activation—compromise cardiac structure and function, thereby facilitating the development of HF, particularly heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, in patients with established CAD ( , ). The main innovations of this study are as follows: First, the multicenter design enhances the generalizability of the findings to a broader population. Second, this study is the first to systematically demonstrate, in a high-risk CAD cohort, that all four obesity-metabolic indices—TyG, TyG-BMI, TyG-WC, and METS-IR—are significantly associated with HF and exhibit clear threshold effects, providing a valuable reference range for future risk stratification. Finally, comparative analyses revealed that METS-IR possesses the best diagnostic performance for HF in CAD patients, and mediation analysis further suggested that its association with HF may be partly mediated through renal function. This provides a rationale for weight management and improvement of IR to preserve renal function and potentially reduce HF risk. This study also has several limitations. First, since our study only included patients from the Chinese population, caution should be exercised when generalizing our findings to other populations, regions, or ethnic groups. Further validation studies in diverse geographic regions and different ethnic populations are warranted. Second, all obesity-metabolic indices were calculated based on data collected during the first hospitalization, and their dynamic changes and potential influence on HF could not be assessed; future studies should explore this aspect further. Thirdly, given the inherent nature of observational studies, causal inference is not feasible. Therefore, the findings of the current study should be interpreted as demonstrating an association between the obesity-metabolic indices and HF, and causal relationships can only be established through large-scale prospective cohort studies or rigorous randomized controlled trials in the future. Fourth, although extensive confounding factors were adjusted for, unmeasured confounding may still exist; however, E-value analysis suggested that such influence on the main conclusions is likely limited. 5 Conclusion This study found that all four obesity-metabolic indices were significantly associated with HF in patients with CAD, exhibiting a clear threshold effect. Notably, when METS-IR exceeded 38.5, its association with HF was significantly enhanced. Moreover, METS-IR demonstrated superior diagnostic performance and may promote HF through renal function impairment. Of course, as this was an observational study, inherent limitations such as potential reverse causality preclude definitive conclusions regarding causal relationships. Therefore, large-scale, multicenter, prospective cohort studies or randomized controlled trials focusing on metabolic and weight-loss interventions are warranted to further validate and extend our findings.

Identifying prognostic factors for long-term outcomes in ST-segment Elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI) patients after successful Percutaneous Coronary Intervention (PCI) is critical to improving survival. The Triglyceride-Glucose (TyG) index, a surrogate marker of insulin resistance derived from fasting glucose and triglyceride levels, has been widely used in cardiovascular risk assessment [ – ]. However, most studies focus on single-timepoint measurements, overlooking the prognostic significance of dynamic changes over time. Given that the TyG index fluctuates with metabolic status, analyzing its longitudinal trajectories could better capture its association with prognosis. Group-Based Trajectory Modeling (GBTM) is a statistical method that identifies distinct developmental trajectories within heterogeneous populations [ – ]. Unlike traditional growth models, GBTM captures interindividual variability by classifying patients into subgroups based on trajectory patterns. This approach has potential to improve risk stratification in STEMI patients by revealing how different TyG index trajectories relate to clinical outcomes. In this study, we applied GBTM to longitudinal TyG data from STEMI patients undergoing PCI to identify distinct trajectory groups and investigate their associations with long-term prognosis. Study population This retrospective cohort study included 1,092 patients with acute ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) who were hospitalized in the Department of Cardiology at the Affiliated Hospital of Hebei University and underwent emergency coronary angiography between October 2013 and October 2018.Inclusion criteria: Patients meeting the 2010 Chinese diagnostic criteria for acute STEMI [ , ]. Exclusion criteria were as follows: patients with end-stage renal disease or requiring dialysis; severe hepatic failure; active malignancy or a life expectancy less than one year; severe infectious diseases; other severe systemic diseases significantly impacting prognosis; and those with missing key clinical data, including fasting glucose and triglyceride levels. This retrospective cohort study initially screened 1,200 patients with acute STEMI who underwent primary PCI at our hospital. According to the exclusion criteria, 24 patients were excluded due to end-stage renal disease or dialysis dependence, severe hepatic failure, active malignancy or life expectancy < 1 year, severe infections, or other systemic conditions significantly affecting prognosis. Additionally, 30 patients were excluded due to missing key clinical data (such as fasting glucose or triglyceride levels), and 54 patients were excluded due to loss to follow-up or incomplete TyG-related follow-up data. A total of 1,092 patients were included in the final analysis. Patient selection is detailed in the flowchart (Fig. ). This study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Affiliated Hospital of Hebei University (Approval No. HDFYLL-KY-2023-080). As this was a retrospective study using anonymized medical records, the requirement for written informed consent was waived by the ethics committee. Methods (follow-up and outcome assessment section) The follow-up process consisted of two phases. The first phase was a 12-month structured follow-up period after discharge, during which outpatient visits were scheduled at 3, 6, 9, and 12 months to collect fasting triglyceride and glucose levels. After this period, patients entered a 5-year long-term follow-up phase focused on outcome ascertainment. Long-term follow-up was conducted through a combination of outpatient visits and structured telephone interviews, continuing until the occurrence of a predefined endpoint event or the end of the observation period. Of the 1,146 enrolled patients, 1,092 completed visits, resulting in a follow-up completion rate of 95.2% (Fig. ). All major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) were adjudicated by experienced clinicians and research staff using data from electronic medical records, hospitalization summaries, outpatient documentation, and telephone interviews. In cases of disagreement or uncertainty, a third independent reviewer resolved discrepancies to ensure consistent and accurate classification of events. Definition of anemia: Anemia was defined as a hemoglobin (Hb) level below 115 g/L at admission, regardless of sex. The severity of anemia was not further classified in this study. Primary outcomes MACE was defined as a composite of cardiac death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, target vessel revascularization, and rehospitalization for heart failure. Outcome events were recorded over a 5-year period following the final measurement of fasting triglyceride and glucose levels (i.e., post-12-month assessment). GBTM was conducted using R software, and the selection of the optimal number of trajectory groups was based on the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC), average posterior probability (AvePP), minimum group proportion (≥ 5%), and odds of correct classification (OCC). A lower BIC indicates better model fit, AvePP > 0.7 suggests good classification accuracy, and OCC > 5 reflects strong discriminative power of the model. The final trajectory grouping was determined by a comprehensive evaluation of statistical criteria, clinical plausibility, and interpretability, aiming to accurately characterize the dynamic patterns of the TyG index in acute STEMI patients who underwent successful percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) during follow-up. Group-based trajectory modeling analyses and trajectory plots were performed using R software. Kaplan-Meier survival analysis was used to estimate differences in clinical outcomes across TyG trajectory groups, and the log-rank test was applied to evaluate the significance of group differences. Cox proportional hazards regression models were used to assess the association between TyG trajectory patterns and clinical outcomes. For pairwise comparisons among the three trajectory groups, Bonferroni correction was applied, and adjusted p-values < 0.017 were considered statistically significant. For other analyses, a two-sided p-value < 0.05 was regarded as statistically significant. All analyses were based on complete cases, and patients with missing key data were excluded from the corresponding analyses. No imputation was performed. In addition, as shown in Fig. , the trajectories in the four- and five-group models exhibited considerable overlap, with poor differentiation between groups, making subsequent analysis and interpretation less reliable. Considering the model fit, trajectory clarity, and clinical relevance, a three-trajectory model was ultimately selected. Trajectory 1 (persistently high group; n = 92) included patients whose TyG index started at a relatively high level and showed no significant decline over time. Trajectory 2 (moderate level group; n = 196) consisted of patients with a moderate baseline TyG level that remained relatively stable without a significant decrease. Trajectory 3 (rapid decline group; n = 804) included patients whose TyG index started at a moderate level but declined rapidly over the follow-up period (Fig. ). Significant differences were observed in serum uric acid and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) levels among the three groups. Group-wise comparisons of survival outcomes also revealed statistically significant differences (Table ). Selection of covariates Variables with statistically significant differences in baseline characteristics across the three trajectory groups were identified. The selection of confounding factors in this study was based on variables with a P value less than 0.05 in intergroup comparisons, as well as clinically recognized risk factors supported by clinical experience and relevant literature. Covariates included sex, age, LDL-c, uric acid, BMI, hypertension, diabetes, family history of coronary heart disease, smoking status, multivessel disease, ejection fraction, Killip class, GFR, fasting blood glucose, triglycerides, baseline TyG index, and final TyG index. Multicollinearity diagnostics Before conducting multivariate Cox regression analysis, multicollinearity among triglycerides (TG), fasting blood glucose (FBG), and the TyG index was assessed. The tolerance values for TG and FBG were both 0.991, and the corresponding variance inflation factor (VIF) values were 1.009, indicating no evidence of multicollinearity. Although the TyG index is calculated based on TG and FBG, it represents a nonlinear transformation. In addition, TG and FBG showed a dispersed distribution in this cohort. Therefore, TG, FBG, and the TyG index were considered statistically independent and were eligible for inclusion in the multivariate model. Association between trajectory groups and prognosis As shown in Tables , , , and , both unadjusted and adjusted Cox regression analyses demonstrated that the trajectory group was independently associated with prognosis ( P < 0.05 in all models). In individuals with normal glucose metabolism, activation of insulin receptors triggers signaling to IRS-1 (insulin receptor substrate-1), which then interacts with and activates the downstream PI3-kinase (PI3K, a p85/p110 complex). This leads to activation of Akt, promoting the translocation of GLUT4 to the cell membrane and facilitating glucose uptake into cells for metabolism. Additionally, this pathway activates nitric oxide synthase (NOS), promoting vasodilation and maintaining endothelial function. In patients with hyperglycemia, impaired IRS-1 signaling results in reduced glucose metabolism and decreased eNOS activity, thereby impairing vasodilation. Meanwhile, the MAP kinase pathway remains sensitive to insulin. The insulin resistance of the IRS-1/PI3K pathway leads to compensatory hyperinsulinemia, which in turn excessively activates the MAPK pathway, promoting inflammation, cellular proliferation, and the progression of atherosclerosis. Dyslipidemia contributes to this process by triggering inflammatory storms mediated by NF-κB and inhibiting IRS-1 function, thus forming a vicious cycle between insulin resistance and atherosclerosis. This association was especially prominent among elderly individuals (HR = 2.15, 95% CI: 1.50–3.07, P < 0.001) [ ]. Similarly, a Korean study confirmed an independent positive correlation between the TyG index and baPWV and showed that the TyG index was superior to HOMA-IR for predicting arteriosclerosis [ ]. Accumulating evidence has shown that the TyG index serves as a reliable predictor for cardiovascular outcomes in various populations. Notably, several nomogram-based models incorporating the TyG index have demonstrated good predictive performance for MACEs in patients with HFpEF post-CABG, new-onset hypertension, STEMI undergoing PCI, and chronic coronary disease. From a systemic pathological perspective, metabolic dysregulation caused by insulin resistance involves multiple tissues and signaling pathways. The underlying mechanisms mainly involve endothelial dysfunction, chronic inflammatory responses, and oxidative stress. Under physiological conditions, insulin regulates blood flow and glucose metabolism by promoting nitric oxide (NO) production in vascular endothelial cells. However, in the IR state, NO synthesis is reduced, impairing vascular relaxation function [ ]. In addition, IR can induce the sustained release of pro-inflammatory cytokines, such as interleukin-6 (IL-6), tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), and C-reactive protein (CRP), as well as reactive oxygen species (ROS). These processes mutually reinforce each other, forming a vicious cycle of “inflammation-oxidative stress,” which further aggravates endothelial injury [ , ]. Meanwhile, a persistently elevated TyG index may also disrupt insulin secretion, promote myocardial fibrosis and left ventricular hypertrophy, ultimately leading to cardiac dysfunction [ ]. These pathological changes not only impair myocardial structure and function but may also destabilize coronary plaques and increase the risk of thrombosis. Furthermore, studies have shown that IR and hyperinsulinemia can activate serum/glucocorticoid-regulated kinase 1 (SGK1) through multiple signaling pathways and stimulate aldosterone secretion, which in turn further activates SGK1. As a shared node in insulin and aldosterone signaling, SGK1 increases intracellular sodium ion concentration in vascular smooth muscle cells by activating sodium channels, while inhibiting nitric oxide synthase activity and reducing NO production. This cascade ultimately leads to increased vascular tone, endothelial dysfunction, and vascular stiffening [ ]. In addition, the TyG index may contribute to the development of coronary artery disease (CAD) through its roles in dyslipidemia, diabetes, and hypertension, highlighting its central role in metabolic syndrome [ , ]. Concurrently, hyperinsulinemia abnormally activates the MAPK pathway, promoting inflammation and vascular smooth muscle cell proliferation, which accelerates atherosclerosis. Lipid dysregulation further aggravates insulin resistance via NF-κB–mediated inflammatory cascades and inhibition of IRS-1 signaling, creating a vicious cycle in the progression of atherosclerosis. As a composite indicator reflecting the metabolic burden of both glucose and lipid dysregulation, the TyG index may more sensitively capture these interactive abnormalities and underlying metabolic stress. Trajectory-based monitoring of the TyG index can provide a more accurate prediction of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) and assist in formulating more proactive metabolic management and cardiovascular protection strategies. These findings indicate that a single measurement of the TyG index is insufficient for comprehensive risk assessment, and regular monitoring of its trajectory may improve the accuracy of prognosis prediction. Future studies could explore the incorporation of the TyG trajectory into existing STEMI risk assessment models and evaluate the effectiveness of targeted interventions. Overall, as a simple and effective metabolic biomarker, the TyG index demonstrates considerable value for the early identification and personalized management of cardiovascular disease. Limitations and future perspectives This study revealed an association between TyG index trajectories and long-term prognosis in patients with STEMI; however, several limitations should be acknowledged: Study design and generalizability This study employed a single-center retrospective design, which limits the generalizability of the findings and may introduce selection bias. Nevertheless, the inclusion of 1,092 patients provides a relatively large sample size with considerable representativeness, enhancing the robustness of the conclusions. Lack of detailed medication information and potential confounding Information on glucose-lowering medication use was not collected. As such treatments can affect fasting glucose levels and indirectly influence the TyG index, the absence of these data may introduce unmeasured confounding. Moreover, the definition of “regular medication use” was based on patient self-reporting, and the retrospective nature of data collection may have led to bias in assessing medication adherence. Future prospective studies should collect detailed medication data to explore the impact of antidiabetic therapy on TyG trajectories and cardiovascular outcomes. Inclusion of patients with specific metabolic disorders This study did not exclude patients with severe hypertriglyceridemia or familial chylomicronemia syndrome, which may affect the accuracy of the TyG index in cardiovascular risk assessment. Although elevated triglyceride levels in these patients are typically related to acute pancreatitis rather than atherosclerosis, their specific impact on cardiovascular risk prediction remains unclear. Future studies should consider excluding or separately analyzing these patients to improve the applicability and predictive performance of the TyG index in diverse populations. Limited dynamic monitoring during the acute phase During hospitalization for acute myocardial infarction, triglyceride and fasting glucose levels are typically measured only at admission and at limited time points, lacking close monitoring of dynamic changes during the acute phase. This limitation mainly arises from routine clinical diagnostic and treatment procedures and the complex physiological status of patients in the acute phase. Therefore, this study could not capture the dynamic changes of the TyG index during the acute phase, representing an important limitation. Future studies should consider dynamic monitoring during the acute phase to better characterize these changes and their clinical implications. However, these time points lacked systematic, evidence-based justification, which may limit a comprehensive understanding of TyG dynamic patterns. Additionally, some patients were lost to follow-up, potentially introducing attrition bias and affecting result reliability. Future multicenter, large-sample studies should design more rigorous follow-up protocols and minimize loss to follow-up to better capture the clinical significance of TyG changes. Research insights What is currently known about this topic? The triglyceride-glucose (TyG) index is a validated surrogate marker of insulin resistance and is associated with cardiovascular risk. Most previous studies have relied on single-timepoint measurements of the TyG index, which may not capture its dynamic metabolic changes. Dynamic metabolic markers may provide better prognostic information than static measurements. What is the key research question? How do longitudinal trajectories of the TyG index after PCI in STEMI patients affect their long-term cardiovascular outcomes? What is new? Using group-based trajectory modeling, three distinct TyG trajectories—persistently high, moderate, and rapidly declining—were identified in a large STEMI cohort. Patients with a rapid decline in TyG index had significantly lower rates of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE). TyG trajectory was found to be an independent predictor of long-term prognosis. How might this study influence clinical practice? Dynamic monitoring of TyG trajectories may enable improved risk stratification and personalized secondary prevention in STEMI patients.

chunks.content: 1 Introduction The number of critically ill patients with coronary artery disease undergoing high-risk percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) supported by mechanical circulatory support (MCS) devices such as the microaxial flow-pump Impella (Abiomed by J&J, Danvers, Massachusetts) has steadily increased over the past decade. The relevance of this topic was underscored by the recent DanGer Shock trial, which showed a mortality reduction when Impella support was added to standard care in STEMI patients with cardiogenic shock. PCI mandates dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) with acetylsalicylic acid and an oral P2Y 12 inhibitor (P2Y 12 i) to prevent ischemic complications, including early stent thrombosis. However, this benefit is offset by an increased risk of bleeding. Managing antiplatelet therapy in critically ill patients is particularly challenging: the efficacy of oral P2Y 12 i may be compromised by impaired gastrointestinal absorption and hepatic metabolism in the setting of hemodynamic instability and organ hypoperfusion. Moreover, Impella support itself increases bleeding risk through thrombocytopenia and proteolysis of von Willebrand factor. Cangrelor, an intravenous P2Y 12 i, provides rapid, potent, and quickly reversible platelet inhibition, making it an attractive option for critically ill PCI patients at high ischemic and bleeding risk. Beyond its pharmacokinetic advantages, recent studies have further clarified both the strengths and limitations of cangrelor in real–world PCI. While it ensures immediate platelet suppression during PCI, variability in platelet reactivity may occur during transition to oral agents, depending on timing and the choice of oral P2Y 12 i. Pharmacodynamic comparisons also suggest that glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors may achieve even more potent early platelet inhibition than cangrelor, underscoring the need to individualize intravenous antiplatelet strategies. . Two randomized clinical trials have demonstrated potential advantages of cangrelor over selected oral P2Y 12 i. , In CHAMPION–PHOENIX, cangrelor significantly reduced the primary ischemic composite endpoint compared with clopidogrel. In DAPT–SHOCK–AMI, cangrelor reduced the secondary ischemic composite endpoint compared with ticagrelor, although the primary endpoint was not met. Despite these findings, evidence supporting cangrelor use in patients undergoing PCI with mechanical circulatory support remains limited. , In this context, we compared outcomes of DAPT with oral P2Y 12 i alone versus cangrelor loading among real-world patient cohort requiring Impella–supported PCI. 2 Methods 2.1 Study setting and population We analyzed data from consecutive patients enrolled in an observational mechanical circulatory support (MCS) device registry ( NCT04117230 ) at the Heart Center of the Luzerner Kantonsspital, Luzern, Switzerland, which serves as the tertiary cardiology facility for the central region of Switzerland. Between 2015 and 2019, data were collected retrospectively, and from August 2019 onward, data were collected prospectively. We included virtually all patients who underwent protected or urgent PCI supported by an Impella microaxial flow pump (Abiomed by J&J, Danvers, MA) at our institution between 2015 and 2025. Exclusion criteria were age < 18 years or refusal of consent. For the current analysis, we additionally excluded patients presenting with cardiogenic shock requiring MCS due to non–ischemic causes (e.g., Takotsubo syndrome, cardiac arrhythmia, valvular heart disease, acute heart failure, or acute myocarditis). 2.2 Data collection and event adjudication Data was collected by trained study personnel and entered into an electronic database (REDCap, Vanderbilt University, Nashville, TN). Information included demographics, medical history, cardiovascular risk factors, indication for hospital admission and device implantation, procedural characteristics, periprocedural antithrombotic regimen, periprocedural complications within 48h, in-hospital outcomes, and 6-month clinical events. Follow-up data were obtained through scheduled outpatient visits or by structured telephone interviews. In addition, institutional electronic medical records and reports from out-patient cardiologists or other specialists were systematically reviewed. When follow-up information was incomplete or missing, patients’ relatives or referring physicians were contacted by telephone to ascertain the occurrence of any post-discharge events. If a potential event was identified, relevant source documents (e.g., hospital reports, procedural reports, or imaging findings) were retrieved. Each follow-up event was documented in a dedicated follow-up event record and adjudicated accordingly. All study outcomes were adjudicated by two independent investigators (experienced physicians) who were not involved in the clinical management of the patients. Any discrepancies were resolved by consensus with a senior investigator. 2.3 Outcomes of interest The objective was to compare the incidence of periprocedural complications within 48h, in-hospital outcomes as well as 6-month clinical events between patients undergoing Impella-supported PCI treated with DAPT using oral P2Y 12 i only versus loading with cangrelor followed by oral P2Y 12 i. In-hospital outcomes included: mean intermediate care unit (ICU) length of stay, transfusion requirements (packed red blood cells and platelet concentrates), early stent thrombosis, target lesion revascularization (TLR), target vessel revascularization, revascularization of another vessel, recurrent MI, ischemic or hemorrhagic cerebrovascular insult (CVI), coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG), all-cause mortality, cardiovascular (CV) mortality, and major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE). MACE was defined as a composite of recurrent MI, CVI, and CV mortality. 6-month clinical events included MI, CVI, repeat PCI, TLR, all-cause mortality, CV mortality and MACE. The primary outcomes comprised periprocedural major bleeding (BARC ≥ 3) within 48h, in-hospital MACE and 6-month MACE. 2.4 Antithrombotic management Our local practice generally follows contemporaneous international guideline recommendations for the management of acute and chronic coronary disease. , , , , , , , , , , , , Dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) consisted of aspirin plus a loading dose of a P2Y 12 i, administered either orally (clopidogrel, prasugrel, or ticagrelor) or intravenously as cangrelor, followed by maintenance therapy. The choice of antiplatelet regimen in each case was left to the treating physician and was influenced by the patient’s clinical condition, age, comorbidities, and the estimated ischemic and bleeding risk. Over the study period, a temporal shift in P2Y 12 i selection was observed in patients with acute coronary syndromes, with decreasing use of clopidogrel and increasing use of the more potent agents prasugrel and ticagrelor . For cangrelor administration, we followed the manufacturer’s instructions for use. Patients treated with cangrelor received a 30 µg/kg bolus followed by a continuous infusion of 4 µg/kg/min, according to the CHAMPION‑PLATFORM study protocol After the PCI procedure and once clinical stabilization was achieved, patients treated with cangrelor were transitioned to an oral P2Y 12 i Patients on cangrelor received a loading dose of ticagrelor (180 mg) and the cangrelor infusion was continued for at least 30 min. For patients not eligible for ticagrelor loading, a loading dose of clopidogrel (600 mg) was given and the cangrelor infusion was discontinued. In our practice, for patients receiving oral P2Y12 inhibitor loading only, we generally administer the loading dose of the preferred agent—ticagrelor, prasugrel, or clopidogrel—once the coronary anatomy and PCI strategy have been defined directly in the catheterization laboratory during the PCI procedure. Treatment with oral P2Y 12 i is typically continued for 6–12 months. All patients received unfractionated heparin during PCI to maintain an activated clotting time (ACT) > 250 s. 2.5 Implantation and management of microaxial flow pump The Impella microaxial flow pump was implanted fully percutaneously via the femoral artery using 12 Fr (Impella 2.5) or 14 Fr (CP) sheaths. Ultrasound guidance was used if possible. Whenever feasible, a single-access–only strategy was adopted, using the same femoral arterial access for both Impella implantation and PCI in order to minimize additional vascular punctures. The device was inserted over a stiff 0.018-inch guidewire, advanced under fluoroscopy, and positioned retrogradely across the aortic valve. Impella was explanted as soon as clinically feasible based on the patient’s hemodynamic status. 2.6 PCI procedures For PCI procedures at our institution, all interventions were performed in accordance with current international guideline recommendations. , Lesion preparation was typically achieved using pre-dilatation with semi- or non-compliant balloons. Additional devices such as modified balloons, atherectomy, or intravascular lithotripsy were used when indicated. Latest-generation drug-eluting stents were routinely implanted. Direct stenting was reserved for selected cases, while thrombectomy was performed as a bailout strategy or for large thrombus burden (TIMI 4–5). Institutional standards encouraged liberal use of intravascular imaging for lesion characterization and/or stent optimization. Post-dilatation was generally performed with appropriately sized non-compliant balloons at high pressure (>18 atm) to ensure optimal stent expansion and apposition. 2.7 Statistical analysis Categorical data are reported as frequencies and percentages, whereas continuous variables are presented as mean ± standard deviations when distributions were not heavily skewed or when the mean was considered more informative, and as median with interquartile range when skewed with extreme outliers. Statistical comparisons were conducted using Pearson's chi-square test or Fisher's exact test for categorical variables and either Student's t -test, the Wilcoxon rank-sum test, or the Wilcoxon exact test for continuous variables, depending on distributional assumptions and sample size. To address confounding by indication, propensity scores for receiving cangrelor were estimated using logistic regression including clinically relevant baseline characteristics associated with treatment allocation (cardiogenic shock, cardiac arrest, STEMI, elective high-risk protected PCI, age, and sex). Stabilised inverse probability of treatment weights (IPTW) were computed to estimate the average treatment effect. Covariate balance was assessed using absolute standardised mean differences (threshold < 0.1). IPTW-adjusted treatment effects were estimated using weighted logistic regression with robust standard errors for binary outcomes and weighted Cox regression with robust variance for 6-month MACE; the proportional hazards assumption was verified using Schoenfeld residuals. Sensitivity analyses included weight trimming at the 99th percentile, average treatment effect on the treated (ATT) estimation, and an expanded propensity score model additionally including left ventricular ejection fraction and SCAI shock stage. Exploratory subgroup analyses assessed whether treatment effects differed by cardiogenic shock status, STEMI presentation, and age (above/below the median). Within each stratum, binary outcomes were compared using Fisher's exact test and logistic regression, while 6-month MACE was compared using the log-rank test and Cox regression. Treatment-by-subgroup interaction was tested using Wald tests for the interaction term in pooled models. No correction for multiple testing was applied. Events-per-variable (EPV) ratios and effective sample sizes after IPTW weighting were calculated for all multivariable models to assess model adequacy. A two-tailed p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Descriptive analyses and regression models were performed using R version 4.4.1 (R Core Team, 2024). Participants were informed about the observational nature of the study, including clinical or telephone follow-ups, and written consent was obtained whenever possible.
